candidates.title: Precision, Pragmatism, and Emerging Paradigms in Determining Kidney Filtration Function
candidates.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined largely by glomerular filtration rate (GFR), a construct with broad clinical implications. Guidelines from Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes categorize CKD stages in adults according to GFR thresholds and albuminuria to assess risk of kidney failure. These CKD categories help clinicians dose medications with a narrow therapeutic window (eg, chemotherapy, antimicrobials), screen for metabolic complications of kidney dysfunction, determine eligibility for kidney transplant, and evaluate risks of death and cardiovascular disease events. Yet a patient’s GFR assessment depends on which test is ordered. In routine clinical practice, GFR is estimated (eGFR) rather than measured (mGFR). Small differences between estimates for GFR that fall close to the thresholds for CKD categorization can reclassify a patient’s disease status, thereby influencing diagnostic testing and treatment decisions. Measured GFR is the reference standard, but it is burdensome, time consuming, and not widely available. Thus, most clinical studies rely on eGFR to determine the associations of CKD with kidney failure, cardiovascular disease, and death.

candidates.abstract: To the Editor We welcome the report of the ORCHESTRA randomized clinical trial (RCT) that investigated the effect on overall survival from debulking of metastases after first-line systemic treatment in patients with stage 4 CRC. The trial reported no difference between the 2 groups for the primary outcome of overall survival. PulMiCC, a phase 3 RCT of surgical resection of CRC lung metastases, reached the same conclusion, but, surprisingly, Dr Gootjes and colleagues did not mention it. The editorialist opined that “ORCHESTRA hits a sour note.” We take a contrary view: ORCHESTRA rings true.

candidates.title: Tumor Debulking Plus Chemotherapy for Multiorgan Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
candidates.abstract: To the Editor The ORCHESTRA trial addressed the evolving role of local therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). The authors should be commended for their rigorous evaluation of debulking in this challenging setting. The study required that patients have metastases in at least 2 different organs. However, patients had metastatic sites with very different prognoses (eg, lungs, bone, peritoneum). In such widely disseminated disease, progression of the less favorable site inevitably determines survival. We are concerned that the induction systemic therapy was brief—only 3 to 4 cycles—using only capecitabine and oxaliplatin with or without bevacizumab or folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin with or without bevacizumab. Given advanced metastatic disease, these regimens appear insufficient to reliably ensure good control of the systemic disease. Compounding this issue, patients who achieved merely stable disease (vs an objective response) were included. To select candidates who might genuinely benefit from local therapies, a longer induction period leading to a sustained objective response to chemotherapy for a period of at least 3 months is essential.

candidates.title: Choosing Distance: Medical Professionalism and Poetry
candidates.abstract: Poetry, through its visceral immediacy and catalyzing of human emotion, has the power to close distances. Many argue that recent technological advancement has created the opposite, a loss of interpersonal connection, but the experience of alienation or simply growing apart is innate to the human condition, sometimes necessarily accompanying personal growth. In fact, developing professional relationships within health care has long grappled with fostering appropriate distance between physicians and patients, who share intimate, health-related details of their lives, or among physician colleagues, who often witness stressful events together but ultimately must confront such burdens alone. The poem “Distance Learning” provides an example of a clinician in training questioning distance, although ironically not the type enforced by the hospital workplace setting. Instead, the speaker remarks on “a distance I chose” from her own family in seeking medical training. Using tender, homespun imagery juxtaposed against her rigorous hospital duties, the realities of her vocation strain against the comforts of sitting around a familiar table, being with caring parents, and experiencing uninterrupted, unabashed closeness with her loved ones. The poem acknowledges that problematic, well-known ethos in medicine that career always takes priority—physicians must eat, drink, and sleep medicine—creating tension between its duties and physicians’ other needs and interests. Yet in a poem that elicits the pains and sacrifices of pursuing medical training, we still find an accessible, paradoxically forgiving space that helps bridge emotional distance when physical closeness seems impossible.
